passage.title: The Architect’s Son
paras: For most of Yasir’s childhood, his father had been a voice on the phone and a name on the side of buildings. As one of the country’s leading architects, he designed towers in Riyadh and hotels in Jeddah, and he was always on his way to somewhere else.

Yasir had learned not to ask when he would be home. At his school prize-giving, the seat beside his mother was empty again. Afterwards, his father called to apologise. Yasir said, “It’s fine,” in the flat voice he had perfected, and ended the call first.

In the summer Yasir turned fifteen, his father had a mild heart attack and was ordered to rest for three months. For the first time, he was home all day. Yasir avoided him. He did not know how to be angry at a man who now moved so slowly.

One afternoon, looking for a charger, Yasir opened the door of his father’s study and stopped. On the desk stood a scale model of a small, ordinary house with a courtyard and a single palm tree. It was meticulous: tiny windows, a wooden door, even a bicycle leaning against the wall.

“That’s our first house,” his father said from the doorway. “In Unaizah. You were four. You used to ride that bicycle round and round the palm.” He paused. “I build towers for strangers. I made this one for me. I wanted to remember the years I was actually there.”
Yasir looked at the little bicycle for a long time. Then he pulled out the chair beside the desk. “Show me how you made the windows,” he said.

items.stem: What does Yasir’s “flat voice he had perfected” suggest about him?
options: He is practising to become a professional speaker.
He has learned to hide his disappointment behind indifference.
He does not really care whether his father comes home.
He has a medical problem that affects the way he speaks to people.
items.skill: Determines details that reveal characters’ thoughts

items.stem: Why does Yasir avoid his father after the heart attack?
options: He is caught between long-held anger and new sympathy for a weakened man.
He is afraid that his father will ask him to study architecture.
He wants to punish his father for missing the prize-giving ceremony last year.
He has been told by the doctor not to disturb his father.
items.skill: Analyzes how a character responds to complex situations

items.stem: What is the significance of the scale model?
options: It proves that his father prefers small houses to large towers.
It shows that his father is planning to build a new and much larger house for the family.
It reveals that his father values the family years he missed and regrets his absence.
It explains why his father became interested in architecture as a boy.
items.skill: Interprets symbolism in literary text

items.stem: What contrast does the father draw in the line “I build towers for strangers. I made this one for me”?
options: between his own building designs and those of other famous architects
between the cost of towers and the cost of houses
between the cities of Riyadh and Unaizah
between his public work and his private, personal memories
items.skill: Analyzes dialogue to understand characters

items.stem: How does Yasir’s final request show a change in him?
options: He chooses to connect with his father through something they can share.
He wants to fix the model because it has been damaged.
He wants to prove that he can build better windows.
He decides that he wants to become an architect like his father one day.
items.skill: Understands how characters are developed or changed

items.stem: Which statement BEST expresses a theme of the story?
options: Scale models are the best way to remember a family home.
Children should forgive their parents for anything they do.
Successful careers always damage family relationships beyond any hope of repair.
Understanding another person’s regrets can open a path to reconciliation.
items.skill: Analyzes the development of theme in literary text

passage.title: The Guest Book
paras: Murad’s family ran a small guesthouse in the mountains near Al-Baha, and every evening Murad read the guest book aloud to his mother while she cooked. Most entries were kind: thanks for the bread, praise for the view, drawings of the terraced fields by children.
One evening, he stopped reading. A guest had written, in sharp, slanting letters: “The rooms are cold, the water is weak and the owners talk too much. I will not return.”
Murad felt his face burn. His mother had been up since five; his father had carried that guest’s heavy suitcase up three flights of stairs. He reached for a pen to cross the entry out.
His mother caught his wrist. “Leave it,” she said.
“But it’s unfair!”

“Some of it,” she agreed. “But read it again.” He did. “The rooms are cold,” she repeated. “Are they?” Murad thought of the broken heater on the second floor, the one his father kept promising to fix. “The water is weak.” The pump. Also on the list. She stirred the pot. “A guest who is angry tells you what a guest who is polite will not.”

The next week, Murad and his father fixed the heater and replaced the pump. Murad left the harsh entry in the book. Beneath it, months later, a new guest wrote: “Warm rooms, strong water, and owners who talk just enough.”

items.stem: Why does Murad want to cross out the entry?
options: He is embarrassed by the guest’s untidy handwriting.
He feels the criticism is unfair to his hardworking parents.
He thinks the angry guest has written in the wrong book by mistake.
He believes the guest was writing about another hotel.
items.skill: Explains character motivation

items.stem: What does the mother’s reply “Some of it” reveal about her?
options: She agrees completely with every single thing the angry guest wrote in the book.
She wants Murad to apologise to the guest.
She is too tired to argue with her son about it.
She can separate the unfair parts of criticism from the useful parts.
items.skill: Analyzes dialogue to understand characters

items.stem: What does the mother mean by “A guest who is angry tells you what a guest who is polite will not”?
options: Harsh feedback can reveal problems that polite people hide.
Polite guests are more honest than angry ones.
Angry guests should never be allowed to stay at the hotel again.
Guests should always be told what to write.
items.skill: Determines the meaning of a nonliteral phrase

items.stem: Which theme does the story develop?
options: Children should not read guest books aloud.
Guesthouses high in the mountains are always cold in the winter.
Criticism, even when unpleasant, can be a source of growth.
Polite guests are the most valuable customers.
items.skill: Analyzes the development of theme in literary text

items.stem: Why does the author use short, fragmented sentences such as “The pump. Also on the list.”?
options: to show that Murad is far too angry with the guest to speak or think clearly
to show Murad’s thoughts quickly recognising the truth in the criticism
to list the items that the guest stole from the room
to describe the noises made by the old pump
items.skill: Analyzes how sentence structure contributes to meaning

items.stem: Why does Murad leave the harsh entry in the book?
options: It now represents a lesson that led to real improvements.
He forgot about it after fixing the heater.
His mother has forbidden him from ever touching the book again.
He wants future guests to know the rooms were cold.
items.skill: Understands how characters are developed or changed

items.stem: How does the final guest’s entry contribute to the story?
options: It proves that the first guest was lying about the cold rooms and the noisy pump.
It introduces a new problem for the family to solve.
It echoes the harsh review point by point, showing the change it caused.
It proves that the first guest was lying about the rooms.
items.skill: Analyzes how an ending contributes to meaning

passage.title: Diriyah: Where a State Began
paras: On the north-western edge of Riyadh, beside the green line of Wadi Hanifa, stand the mud-brick ruins of At-Turaif, a district of the old town of Diriyah. Its palaces and walls, built in the distinctive Najdi style, may look modest beside the glass towers of the modern capital. Yet this is where the history of the Saudi state began.
**A Capital in the Desert**

In 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud became ruler of Diriyah, and the town became the centre of what historians call the first Saudi state. For nearly a century it grew in power and influence. Its builders used materials suited to the climate: thick mud-brick walls kept rooms cool in summer and warm in winter, and narrow streets provided shade.
**Destruction and Memory**

In 1818, after a long siege, Diriyah was captured and largely destroyed. The capital later moved to Riyadh, and At-Turaif was slowly abandoned. But it was never forgotten. In 2010, At-Turaif was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as an outstanding example of Najdi architecture.
**Restoring the Past**

In recent years, major restoration projects have rebuilt walls and buildings using traditional methods and materials, and museums now tell the district’s story. Since 2022, the Kingdom has marked Founding Day each year on 22 February to commemorate the founding in 1727. Restorers face a difficult balance: making the site welcoming to visitors while keeping it authentic, so that what people see is history rather than imitation.

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Diriyah was captured in 1818 after a long siege and was never rebuilt or visited again by anyone after that.
Founding Day is a national holiday that is celebrated every year in February.
Diriyah’s At-Turaif is a modest-looking but historically central site that is now being carefully restored.
Najdi architecture is more beautiful than the glass towers of modern Riyadh.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: How does the first paragraph introduce the central idea?
options: by contrasting the site’s modest appearance with its great historical importance
by describing in great detail the long and bitter siege that destroyed the town in 1818
by explaining why the capital moved to Riyadh
by listing the materials used to build the palaces
items.skill: Analyzes the purpose of an introduction

items.stem: What does the detail about thick mud-brick walls show about the builders?
options: They built quickly because they feared an attack.
They lacked the materials to build with stone or glass.
They wanted their buildings to look modest to visitors.
They adapted their buildings intelligently to the climate.
items.skill: Makes inferences from informational text

items.stem: How does the section “Destruction and Memory” contribute to the text?
options: It describes the daily life of ordinary people in the first Saudi state.
It explains how the site declined yet remained historically recognised.
It explains how modern museums were built inside the ruins.
It compares Diriyah with other UNESCO sites in the Kingdom.
items.skill: Analyzes how specific sections contribute to meaning

items.stem: What “difficult balance” do restorers face, according to the text?

protecting the ruins while moving them to Riyadh
welcoming visitors while keeping the site authentic
rebuilding quickly while keeping costs as low as possible
items.skill: Analyzes implicit relationships between ideas

items.stem: Which is the BEST objective summary of the text?

Diriyah is the most beautiful and important place in Saudi Arabia, and everyone should visit it at least once to see the old palaces and walk through its narrow streets.
In 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud became ruler of Diriyah, a town beside Wadi Hanifa on the edge of modern Riyadh.
Restorers in Diriyah use traditional methods to rebuild walls, and museums now tell visitors the story of the district.
items.skill: Summarizes informational text

passage.title: Small Pieces, Big Problem: Microplastics
paras: Plastic does not simply disappear. Over time, sunlight, waves and friction break larger pieces into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces smaller than five millimetres are called **microplastics**, and scientists now find them almost everywhere they look: in the deep ocean, in Arctic ice, in soil, in drinking water and even in the air.

Some microplastics come from the breakdown of bottles, bags and fishing nets. Others are released directly: tiny fibres shed from synthetic clothing in the washing machine, and particles worn away from car tyres on the road.

Because they are so small, microplastics are eaten by plankton, fish and shellfish, and they can move up the food chain. Researchers have detected them in human blood and tissues. What this means for health is not yet clear. Studies are under way, but scientists caution that the long-term effects are still uncertain.

Solutions are being explored at many levels. Some countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics. Engineers are designing washing-machine filters to catch fibres. But many researchers argue that the most effective step is the simplest: producing and discarding less plastic in the first place.

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Synthetic clothing is the main source of all plastic pollution in the oceans.
Microplastics are a serious and fully proven cause of illness in most people around the world, so plastic must be banned.
Microplastics are now widespread, their health effects are uncertain, and reducing plastic use is a key solution.
Scientists have found microplastics only in the deep ocean and in Arctic ice.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: How does the second paragraph develop the central idea?
options: by explaining the different sources of microplastics
by defining the size of a microplastic
by listing the countries that have already banned microbeads
by describing the health effects on people
items.skill: Analyzes how specific paragraphs contribute to meaning

items.stem: Why can microplastics move “up the food chain”?
options: Rain lifts them into the air and spreads them.
They float slowly upward from the ocean floor to the surface.
Birds carry them from the sea to the land.
Small animals eat them and are then eaten by larger animals.
items.skill: Analyzes implicit relationships between ideas

items.stem: Which statement about microplastics is supported by the text?
options: All of them come from bottles and bags left on beaches.
Some are released directly from clothing fibres and tyres.
They have been shown to cause disease in humans.
They are larger than five centimetres in size.

items.stem: What does the author’s choice of the word “caution” in the third paragraph signal?
options: careful uncertainty rather than alarm about health effects
complete confidence that microplastics are entirely harmless
strong anger at companies that make plastic
disappointment that research has stopped
items.skill: Analyzes how word choice affects tone

items.stem: What is the author’s purpose in the final paragraph?
options: to describe how plastic is manufactured
to criticise countries that have not banned microbeads
to present a range of responses and highlight the most effective one
to argue that new technology alone can solve the whole problem of pollution
items.skill: Determines specific purpose of a paragraph

items.stem: Which is the BEST objective summary of the text?
options: Microplastics are terrifying, and everyone should immediately stop buying anything that contains plastic, because scientists have proved that they cause serious illness in most people.
Microplastics form when plastic breaks down or is shed from products, spread through the food chain with uncertain health effects, and may be reduced mainly by using less plastic.

items.skill: Summarizes informational text

passage.title: The Precision of Words
paras: Roots reveal meaning: **path** means *feeling*, so **empathy** is the ability to share another person’s feelings, while **apathy** is a lack of feeling or interest.
Tone depends on word choice. A *thrifty* person and a *miserly* person both spend little money, but the first word praises and the second criticises.
An **allusion** draws on shared stories: a “Pyrrhic victory” refers to a king whose victory cost so many soldiers that it was nearly a defeat.
A **paradox** seems contradictory but reveals a truth: “The more you learn, the more you realise how little you know.”

items.stem: The root **path** means “feeling.” A person who shows **apathy** toward a problem —
options: tries hard to solve it
feels deeply about it
does not care about it
understands it fully

passage.title: The Mock Trial
paras: *(A school hall set up as a courtroom for a mock trial. JUDGE (a teacher), PROSECUTOR (HAMAD, 16), DEFENCE (SALEM, 16). The case: a student accused of breaking a science-lab window. The audience already knows, from the opening scene, that the window was broken by a falling branch during a storm.)*
HAMAD: *(confidently)* The defendant was seen near the lab at 4:15. The window was found broken at 4:30. He had motive — he failed his science test that morning. The case is simple.
SALEM: *(standing slowly)* Simple cases are dangerous, Your Honour. They make us stop asking questions. *(He turns to the audience.)* What was the weather like at 4:20?
HAMAD: *(laughing)* Irrelevant.
SALEM: Is it? *(He holds up a photograph.)* This was taken by the caretaker at 4:25. A storm. And this — *(another photograph)* — is the branch lying inside the lab.
*(Silence. HAMAD looks at his notes, then at the photograph.)*
HAMAD: *(quietly, after a pause)* I… withdraw the charge.
JUDGE: *(to the audience)* The verdict, then, is not about this boy. It is about how quickly we decide we already know the answer.

items.stem: How does the opening stage direction create dramatic irony?
options: The audience is told that the judge is secretly a science teacher at the school.
The audience knows that Salem will lose the case.
The audience knows the true cause of the damage while the prosecutor does not.
The audience learns that the defendant failed his science test.
items.skill: Analyzes dramatic irony

items.stem: What does Hamad’s statement “The case is simple” reveal about him?
options: He has reached a conclusion too quickly and with too much confidence.
He wants the trial to end because he is bored.

He has carefully and patiently considered all of the possible evidence.
items.skill: Analyzes dialogue to understand characters

items.stem: What is the effect of Salem’s question about the weather?

It shows that Salem does not really understand the case at all.
It proves immediately that the defendant was not there.
items.skill: Analyzes how dialogue advances plot

items.stem: What tone does the judge’s final line express?

angry and accusing
confused and uncertain
reflective and instructive

items.stem: How do the stage directions *(Silence. HAMAD looks at his notes, then at the photograph.)* affect the pacing?

They slow the scene down at the turning point, letting the impact sink in.
They show that the photographs have been lost.
They speed the scene up so that the trial can end quickly and everyone can leave.
items.skill: Analyzes how structure and pacing create effects

items.stem: What is the central theme of the scene?

Assuming we already know the truth can lead to unjust conclusions.

passage.title: Elegy for the Old Souq
paras: They took the roof of palm and beam,
They took the doors of carved teak brown,
And where the spice-sellers would dream
They laid the marble, cold and clean,
And called it progress for the town.
The new mall glitters, cool and wide;
Its fountains sing a borrowed song.
My father walks its halls with pride,
Then stops beside a pillar’s side
And says, “The cardamom was strong
Right here — or here — I can’t be sure.”
He laughs, but something in him stays
Beside a vanished wooden door,
Inhaling, through a polished floor,
The scent of other, older days.

a poem that gives instructions
a poem that celebrates a victory
a poem that mourns something lost

items.stem: What contrast is developed in the first stanza?

between the warm, handmade old souq and the cold, polished new building
between the spice-sellers in the old souq and the customers who visit them

items.stem: What tone does the phrase “called it progress” create?

passage.title: A Speech to the Graduating Class
paras: Graduates, families, teachers: today you are celebrating an ending. I want to talk about beginnings.

When I was your age, I failed my final mathematics exam. Not by a little — by a lot. I remember walking home, holding the result in my pocket as if it could burn through the fabric. I believed that day that my future had closed. It had not. It had simply changed direction.

You will fail too. Not once, but many times. You will fail at tests, at friendships, at plans you thought were perfect. And each time, you will face the same choice: to stop, or to learn. The world does not reward those who never fall. It rewards those who get up, who look honestly at what went wrong, and who try again — wiser.
Some will tell you that success is about talent. Talent matters. But I have met talented people who became complacent, and ordinary people who became extraordinary through effort. Which will you be?
So aspire high. Work hard. Fail well. And when you stand where I am standing, years from now, I hope you will tell a new class the story of how you got up.

items.stem: What is the speaker’s main purpose?
options: to encourage graduates to treat failure as a step toward growth
to explain how to succeed in mathematics at university
to describe the speaker’s own career in detail
to warn graduates that most of them will fail their first university exams
items.skill: Determines author’s purpose

items.stem: Why does the speaker include the anecdote about failing a mathematics exam?
options: to prove that mathematics is the most difficult subject that students take
to build credibility and show that failure need not end a future
to make the audience laugh at the beginning
to criticise the teachers who marked the exam
items.skill: Analyzes rhetorical devices: anecdote

items.stem: “…holding the result in my pocket as if it could burn through the fabric.” What does this simile convey?
options: the speaker’s fear that the paper would be lost
the speaker’s excitement about the result
the intense shame and anxiety the speaker felt
the hot weather on the day the results came out
items.skill: Analyzes the effect of figurative language

items.stem: Which line uses parallelism MOST clearly?

“It had simply changed direction.”
“Some will tell you that success is about talent.”
“So aspire high. Work hard. Fail well.”

items.stem: How does the speaker address the view that success is about talent?

by changing the subject to the graduates’ families
by accepting that talent matters but arguing that effort can matter more
by agreeing that talent is the only thing that matters
items.skill: Analyzes how an author acknowledges and responds to conflicting views

items.stem: What is the effect of the rhetorical question “Which will you be?”

passage.title: Space Tourism Is Not Worth Its Cost
paras: In recent years, a handful of wealthy people have paid enormous sums for brief trips to the edge of space. Supporters call it the dawn of a new age of exploration. I disagree. Space tourism, at least in its current form, is an expensive luxury the planet cannot afford.

First, consider the environmental cost. Rocket launches release gases and particles high in the atmosphere, where they may linger far longer than pollution at ground level. Scientists are still studying the effects, but a rapid increase in launches for entertainment could add to atmospheric damage.

Second, consider fairness. The price of a single seat could fund clean-water projects for thousands of people. It is difficult to justify such spending on a few minutes of weightlessness for the very rich.

Supporters argue that space tourism drives innovation and will eventually make space travel cheaper for everyone. This is possible: aviation, too, was once only for the wealthy. But aviation developed alongside real practical needs, such as moving mail and cargo. Space tourism, by contrast, offers little benefit beyond the experience itself.
Exploration is noble. Joyrides are not. We should invest in space science that serves humanity, not in brief adventures for the privileged few.

passage.title: Text 1: The Engineer’s Notebook · Text 2: Water Security in the Gulf
paras: **Text 1: The Engineer’s Notebook (a narrative)**

At three in the morning, the alarm on Membrane Line 4 went off again. Engineer Huda Al-Otaibi walked the length of the plant, past the humming pumps, and checked the pressure readings by torchlight. Somewhere beyond the walls, half a million people were asleep, and every one of them would turn on a tap in a few hours without thinking about it. She wrote in her notebook: “Fixed. Again. Nobody will know.” Then she added, after a moment: “That is the point.”
**Text 2: Water Security in the Gulf (an article)**

With few rivers and limited rainfall, Gulf countries depend heavily on desalination for drinking water. Saudi Arabia is among the world’s largest producers of desalinated water. Most modern plants use reverse osmosis, which forces sea water through membranes that block salt. Desalination requires large amounts of energy, and the salty brine it leaves behind must be managed carefully to protect marine life. Because ancient underground aquifers are being used faster than they refill, experts argue that conservation, water recycling and more efficient technology are all essential to long-term water security.

passage.title: Text 1: The Last Pearl Season · Text 2: The Ghawas and the End of an Industry
paras: **Text 1: The Last Pearl Season (a narrative)**

My grandfather made his last dive in the summer the cultured pearls arrived in the markets of Bahrain. He came home with a pouch of small, uneven pearls, the kind that would once have fed us for a month. The merchant offered him a fraction of their worth. “The Japanese grow them now,” the merchant said, “round as moons, cheap as dates.” My grandfather did not argue. He put the pouch in a drawer, where it stayed for forty years, and the next season he found work on a building site in the new oil town. He never spoke of the sea, but every evening he sat facing it.
**Text 2: The Ghawas and the End of an Industry (an article)**

For generations, pearl diving was the backbone of the Gulf economy. Divers, known as *ghawas*, descended repeatedly during the summer season, often with little more than a nose clip and a stone weight. In the 1920s and 1930s, however, cultured pearls produced in Japan began to reach world markets in large numbers, and prices for natural pearls fell sharply. The global economic depression of the 1930s reduced demand further. Within a few decades, the oil industry had replaced pearling as the region’s main source of wealth, and many former divers found new work in construction and the oil fields.

passage.title: The Bus Driver
paras: Every morning, the same driver took Route 12 through the old neighbourhood: a grey-haired man who hummed under his breath and greeted every passenger by name. Talal found it irritating. “He drives like a tortoise,” he complained to his friend. “And why does he care what our names are?”

One morning, a boy at the back was struggling with a mathematics worksheet. The driver, stopped at a red light, glanced in the mirror. “The second one,” he said without turning round. “You’ve multiplied when you should have divided.” The boy checked. He was right.
Talal stared. At the next stop, he asked the old man, half joking, “Were you a teacher?”

“For thirty-one years,” the driver said. “Mathematics. When I retired, the house was too quiet.” He pulled away from the stop slowly, smoothly. “Teaching and driving are not so different,” he added. “Everyone is going somewhere. My job is to get them there safely, even if some of them are in a hurry.”
The next morning, when the bus arrived, Talal said, “Good morning, Ustadh.” The old man smiled and said Talal’s name, as he always had.

passage.title: Lithium: The Metal in Your Pocket
paras: The phone in your pocket, the laptop on your desk and the electric car on the street all have something in common: they depend on batteries made with lithium, the lightest of all metals.

Lithium is valuable for batteries because it stores a great deal of energy for its weight. Lithium-ion batteries can be recharged hundreds of times, which made portable electronics practical and is now helping to make electric vehicles common.

But obtaining lithium has costs. Much of the world’s supply comes from two sources: hard-rock mines, and salt flats in South America where lithium-rich water is pumped into large ponds and left to evaporate. In dry regions, this process uses large amounts of water, which can affect local farmers and ecosystems.

As demand rises, researchers are working on two fronts: finding cleaner ways to extract lithium, and improving recycling so that lithium from old batteries can be used again. The future of clean energy, it seems, depends not only on new technology, but on how responsibly we obtain the materials it needs.

passage.title: The Vizier and the Weaver
paras: A proud vizier once ordered a weaver to make him a carpet “finer than any in the kingdom.” The weaver worked for a year. When the carpet was finished, its colours were deep and its patterns so delicate that people came from far away to see it.
The vizier examined it closely and found, in one corner, a single thread of the wrong colour. “You have ruined it,” he declared, and refused to pay.

The weaver bowed. “My lord,” he said, “that thread is the only one in the carpet that is mine. The other ten thousand belong to the pattern. That one reminds me that I am a man and not the pattern-maker of the world.”

The vizier laughed scornfully and left. That year he made many decisions without listening to anyone, certain that he could not be wrong. Within two years, his mistakes had cost him the sultan’s trust, and he was dismissed.
On his last day in the palace, he passed the weaver’s carpet, now hanging in the great hall. He stopped before the single wrong thread and stood there for a long time.

passage.title: The Juniper Forests of the South
paras: Most people do not picture forests when they think of Saudi Arabia. Yet the high mountains of the south-west, in regions such as Asir and Al-Baha, are home to woodlands of African juniper, evergreen trees that can live for hundreds of years.

These forests do far more than provide shade. Their roots hold soil on steep slopes, reducing erosion. Their branches catch moisture from mountain fog, helping to recharge underground water. They also shelter birds, insects and mammals found in few other places in the Kingdom.

In recent decades, however, scientists have observed many junipers dying back, especially at lower altitudes. Their branches turn brown from the top downward. Researchers point to several possible causes acting together: higher temperatures, changing rainfall, overgrazing by goats and camels that eat young trees, and pressure from roads and construction.

Because juniper seedlings grow slowly, recovery takes time. Conservation efforts include protecting areas from grazing, collecting seeds and growing young trees in nurseries before planting them on the mountains. Scientists stress that these forests, once lost, could take generations to return.

passage.title: The Chess Clock
paras: In the final of the city chess championship, Abdulaziz had seven minutes left on his clock. His opponent, a calm boy from Dammam named Ibrahim, had forty.

Abdulaziz had spent too long on the opening, trying to find a brilliant move instead of a good one. Now every decision felt rushed. His hand hovered over the board. Somewhere behind him, his father coughed.

Then he remembered what his coach had said the week before, when Abdulaziz had lost a practice game the same way: “You are not playing the board. You are playing the clock. Breathe first. A good move made calmly beats a brilliant move made in panic.”
He sat back. He breathed. He looked at the whole board, not just the corner where he had been attacking. There it was: a simple move, nothing brilliant, that protected his king and freed his rook.

He played it with four minutes left. Ibrahim frowned and thought for a long time. Twenty moves later, with eleven seconds on Abdulaziz’s clock, Ibrahim offered a draw. Abdulaziz accepted. Shaking hands across the board, Ibrahim said, “You played the last part like a different person.” Abdulaziz smiled. “I think I was,” he said.

passage.title: The Verdict at the Fountain
paras: *(A village square with an old stone fountain. Two neighbours, ABU FAHD and ABU NAWAF, stand before the village elder, SHEIKH SALIM. A crowd watches.)*
ABU FAHD: My goats drank from this fountain for twenty years. Now he says the water belongs to him because the spring rises on his land.
ABU NAWAF: *(firmly)* It does rise on my land. I paid for the new pipe. Why should his goats drink for free?
SHEIKH SALIM: *(after listening)* Abu Nawaf, who paid for the fountain itself?
ABU NAWAF: *(hesitating)* My grandfather… and his grandfather. Together.

SHEIKH SALIM: So the spring is on your land, and the pipe is yours. But the fountain belongs to both families. *(He turns to the crowd.)* Here is my judgement: Abu Fahd will pay half the cost of the pipe. Abu Nawaf will let the water flow as it always has. And both of you will repair the fountain together, as your grandfathers built it.
*(The two men look at each other. Slowly, ABU NAWAF holds out his hand.)*

items.stem: Why does Sheikh Salim ask who paid for the fountain?

to reveal a shared history that changes how the dispute should be seen
items.skill: Explains character motivation

items.stem: What does the stage direction *(hesitating)* suggest about Abu Nawaf?

items.skill: Analyzes use of stage directions

items.stem: How does Sheikh Salim’s judgement resolve the conflict?
options: It forbids both families from using the fountain in future.

passage.title: For an Old Teacher
paras: You never knew my name, I think;
I was a face in row fourteen,
One of the hundreds at the brink

You wrote one sentence on my page —
“There is a thinker here” — in red;
I kept it like a coin, an age,
Long after other words had fled.
Now I stand where you used to stand
And look at faces, row on row,
And write, with your remembered hand,
The sentences they’ll never know
Are keeping them, like coins, like keys,
Against the long uncertain years —
And I give thanks for fourteen, please,
And for your red ink, and my tears.

passage.title: Paper Comes to Baghdad
paras: For centuries, scholars in the Middle East wrote on papyrus, made from Egyptian reeds, or on parchment, made from animal skin. Papyrus was fragile, and parchment was expensive: a single large book could require the skins of many animals.

Paper-making had been developed in China centuries earlier. According to tradition, the technique reached the Islamic world in the eighth century, and by the end of that century, around 794, a paper mill was operating in Baghdad. Paper was cheaper than parchment and stronger than papyrus, and it could be made from rags and plant fibres.

The effects were far-reaching. Government offices used paper for records and letters. Booksellers’ markets grew, with shops selling copies of works on mathematics, medicine, poetry and religion. Because paper made writing cheaper, more people could own books, and knowledge could be preserved and shared on a scale that had not been possible before.

From Baghdad, paper-making spread west through Damascus and Cairo to North Africa and Spain, and eventually into Europe. Many historians argue that the scholarly achievements of this period would have been far harder without this humble material.

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Baghdad had the largest booksellers’ market in the world.
Papyrus and parchment were the best and most useful writing materials ever made.
The arrival of paper in Baghdad transformed how knowledge was recorded and shared.
China invented paper but never used it for important books.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: How does the first paragraph prepare the reader for the central idea?

by explaining the limitations of earlier writing materials

items.skill: Compares or contrasts details/ideas

passage.title: Close the City Centre to Cars
paras: Our historic city centre should be a place for people. Instead, it is a car park. The city should close the central district to private cars and turn its streets over to pedestrians, cyclists and public transport.

Cities that have tried this have seen clear benefits. When several European cities restricted cars in their centres, studies recorded lower air pollution, fewer road injuries and, in many cases, more visitors to local shops. People who walk past a shop are more likely to stop than people who drive past it.
A car-free centre would also protect our heritage. Vibration and pollution from heavy traffic damage old buildings, and wide roads cut through neighbourhoods that were designed for walking.

Shopkeepers often fear that closing streets to cars will drive customers away. This fear is understandable, but the evidence from many cities suggests the opposite. To ease the change, the city could add park-and-ride stations at the edge of the district and allow deliveries early in the morning.
A city centre full of people, not traffic, is not a dream. It is a choice.

items.stem: What is the author’s claim?

passage.title: The Milkmaids and the Smallpox Vaccine
paras: For centuries, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in the world. It killed a large share of those it infected and left many survivors scarred or blind.

In the eighteenth century, people in parts of England noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, seemed not to catch smallpox. In 1796, the doctor Edward Jenner tested this idea. He took material from a cowpox sore and introduced it into a scratch on the arm of a boy named James Phipps. Weeks later, he exposed the boy to smallpox. The boy did not become ill.

Jenner called his method **vaccination**, from the Latin *vacca*, meaning cow. It spread rapidly across the world. Jenner was not the first to protect people against smallpox; an older practice, which used material from smallpox itself, had long been used in parts of Asia, Africa and the Middle East. But it carried a real risk of causing the disease. Vaccination was much safer.

Nearly two centuries later, after a global vaccination campaign led by the World Health Organization, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the first human disease to be wiped out completely. Today, Jenner’s experiment raises difficult questions: testing a dangerous idea on a child would not be considered ethical now.

items.stem: What observation led to Jenner’s experiment?
options: Cows that ate certain plants in the fields never caught smallpox.

Doctors who treated smallpox rarely became ill.
items.skill: Determines the cause of a situation

items.stem: Where does the word **vaccination** come from, according to the text?

the English word for scratch
the name of the boy Jenner tested
the Latin word for cow
items.skill: Locates details in informational text

items.stem: How is the text mainly organized?
options: chronologically, from the problem through the discovery to its long-term results
as a comparison of the symptoms of smallpox and cowpox in people and in farm animals
as a set of instructions for giving vaccines
as an argument for and against vaccination
items.skill: Identifies chronology as a structure

items.stem: Why does the author mention the older practice used in Asia, Africa and the Middle East?

to argue that the older practice was safer than vaccination
to explain where smallpox first appeared in the world
items.skill: Analyzes how specific details contribute to meaning

passage.title: Why the Dead Sea Is Shrinking
paras: The Dead Sea, which lies between Jordan to the east and Israel and the West Bank to the west, is the lowest point on land on Earth, more than 400 metres below sea level. Its water is so salty that swimmers float easily on the surface. But the lake is in trouble: its level has been falling by about a metre a year.

The main reason is that much less water now reaches it. For thousands of years, the Jordan River fed the Dead Sea. In the twentieth century, countries in the region began diverting much of the river’s water for farming and drinking. At the same time, the Dead Sea loses water through evaporation in the intense heat, and mineral companies pump its water into evaporation ponds to extract potash and other minerals.

The effects can be seen along the shore. As the water retreats, it leaves behind dry land in which thousands of **sinkholes** have formed: sudden collapses in the ground, some large enough to swallow cars or buildings.

Various solutions have been proposed, including a canal or pipeline to bring water from the Red Sea, but they raise questions about cost, environmental risk and cooperation between countries. For now, the Dead Sea continues to shrink.

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Swimmers float easily in the Dead Sea because of its salt.
The Dead Sea is the saltiest, lowest and most beautiful lake anywhere on Earth today.
A canal from the Red Sea has saved the Dead Sea from drying.
The Dead Sea is shrinking mainly because human activity has reduced its water supply.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: How does the third paragraph contribute to the text?
options: It describes a dangerous visible effect of the shrinking lake.
It proposes a solution to the falling water level.
It explains how the lake was formed many millions of years ago.
It describes the minerals extracted from the lake.
items.skill: Analyzes how specific paragraphs contribute to meaning

items.stem: According to the text, which TWO human activities contribute to the falling water level? Choose TWO answers.

passage.title: The Long Silence
paras: When Khalid’s older brother, Fawaz, came home after six years of study in Canada, the whole family went to the airport. Khalid had been ten when Fawaz left. Now he was sixteen, taller than his brother, and suddenly unsure what to say.

At home, everyone talked at once: aunts asking about the snow, cousins asking about the food, their mother asking whether he had eaten properly. Fawaz answered everyone, smiling. Khalid sat at the edge of the room and said nothing.
That night, Khalid found his brother on the roof, looking at the city lights. “You didn’t say anything all evening,” Fawaz said without turning round.
“Everyone else did,” Khalid replied. Then, because the silence felt too large: “You missed everything. My first match. When I broke my arm. When Grandfather—” He stopped.

Fawaz was quiet for a long time. “I know,” he said at last. “I used to call and ask Mother to describe your matches. Every goal. I wrote them down.” He took a worn notebook from his pocket and held it out. On the first page, in his brother’s careful handwriting: *Khalid’s first match. Two assists.*
Khalid turned the pages slowly. Six years of small things, recorded from the other side of the world.

items.stem: What contrast does the author draw between the evening and the roof scene?

passage.title: The Two Merchants of Basra
paras: Two merchants of Basra, Jamil and Rashid, each loaded a ship with dates and sailed for India. Halfway across the sea, a storm struck. Jamil’s crew threw half his cargo overboard to keep the ship afloat. Rashid refused. “Every sack is money,” he said. His ship, too heavy, took on water and sank, and Rashid was rescued with nothing.
In India, Jamil sold what remained of his dates at a good price, for few ships had survived the storm. On his return, he found Rashid begging in the harbour of Basra.
Jamil gave him a sack of silver. “Take it,” he said. “Start again.”
“Why?” asked Rashid bitterly. “You were lucky. I was not.”

“It was not luck,” said Jamil. “I lost half to save the rest. You tried to save everything and lost it all. I give you this not because you deserve it, but so that you may learn the lesson the sea tried to teach us both.”
Rashid took the silver. Years later, when he had become rich again, he was known throughout Basra as the merchant who always knew when to let go.

Of knowledge marked, and blank page earned.

items.stem: How does the third stanza shift the poem’s focus?

from the busy coast to the empty interior of the desert

items.stem: What is the theme of the poem?
options: Intellectual honesty means admitting the limits of one’s knowledge.

passage.title: How Habits Work
paras: Much of what we do each day happens without conscious decision. We brush our teeth, check our phones and take the same route to school almost automatically. Researchers who study behaviour estimate that a large share of daily actions, by some estimates around 40 per cent, are performed out of habit rather than deliberate choice.

Psychologists often describe a habit as a loop with three parts. First comes a **cue**, a signal such as a time of day, a place or a feeling. Then comes the **routine**, the behaviour itself. Finally comes the **reward**, some benefit that makes the brain more likely to repeat the loop next time.

Over time, as the loop is repeated, the behaviour shifts from areas of the brain associated with careful decision-making to areas associated with automatic action. This saves mental effort, which is useful. But it also explains why bad habits are so hard to break: they no longer feel like choices at all.

Research suggests that the most effective way to change a habit is not simply to rely on willpower. Instead, people can change the cue (for example, keeping the phone in another room), or keep the cue and reward but replace the routine with a better one.

passage.title: Projects Should Replace Final Exams
paras: At the end of every term, students cram facts into their memories, write them down in a two-hour exam and forget most of them within weeks. Schools should replace most final exams with extended projects.

Projects measure deeper skills. A two-hour exam rewards students who memorise quickly and perform well under pressure. A project lasting several weeks requires research, planning, problem-solving and the ability to improve work after feedback — the skills universities and employers say they value most.
Projects also reduce harmful stress. Many students report severe anxiety before exams, and a single bad morning can undo a term’s work. A project allows students to show their learning over time.

Critics argue that projects are easier to cheat on, because students can copy from the internet or get help from family. This is a serious concern. However, teachers can require drafts, notes and short oral presentations in which students explain and defend their work. It is difficult to defend work you did not do.
Exams test what students can remember on one day. Projects reveal what they can do. Schools should decide which of these matters more.

In the first half, Majid kept shouting “Pass!” at me, but Majid has never scored more than two goals in a season, so I am not sure why I should have listened to him. In the second half, I scored. A beautiful shot, if I say so myself. After that, I suppose I stopped running back to defend, but that is what defenders are for. When they scored their two goals, both down my side of the pitch, the defenders looked at me as if it were my fault.

Afterwards, nobody spoke to me in the changing room. Coach Nabil said, quietly, “Fourteen shots. One goal. Zero passes.” I think he meant it as a compliment to my shooting. Then he said that I would start the next match on the bench, which shows how little he understands the game.

passage.title: The Stone That Unlocked a Language
paras: For more than a thousand years, no one could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. Travellers admired the elegant symbols on temple walls, but their meaning had been lost.

In 1799, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, known in Europe as Rosetta, found a broken slab of dark stone covered in writing. Scholars quickly realised its importance: it carried the same official decree in three scripts — Egyptian hieroglyphs, a later Egyptian script called Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because scholars could read Greek, the stone offered a key to the other two.

Unlocking that key took more than twenty years. Several scholars made progress, but in 1822 the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced the breakthrough. He showed that hieroglyphs were not simply pictures of ideas, as many had believed, but combined symbols for sounds with symbols for meanings. His knowledge of Coptic, a later form of the Egyptian language, was crucial.

The decipherment opened thousands of years of Egyptian history to modern readers. Today the stone is displayed in the British Museum in London, and its name has become a common phrase for anything that unlocks a difficult problem.

paras: For as long as anyone in the village could remember, old Umm Saleh had kept a lamp burning in her window every night. Children said she was waiting for a ghost. Adults said she was eccentric and wasted oil. Nobody asked her.
Hamdan asked her the year he turned fifteen, when his family sent him each evening to deliver bread to the widows at the edge of the village. He found her trimming the wick.

“My husband went to sea in the winter of the great storm,” she said, “before you were born. His boat was found. He was not.” She set the glass back over the flame. “The first year, I lit it because I hoped. The tenth year, because I could not stop. Now…” She looked out at the dark road. “Now I light it for whoever is coming home late and does not know the way.”

That spring, Hamdan’s cousin, returning from the city on foot after his car broke down in the wadi, followed a single light across three kilometres of dark hills to the village. He arrived at Umm Saleh’s door, exhausted, at two in the morning.
When Umm Saleh died two years later, the village held a meeting about her house. At the end of it, without anyone quite deciding, Hamdan found himself carrying a can of oil up her steps at dusk.

passage.title: The Lamp
paras: Knowledge, my teacher said, is not a sun
That floods the world and leaves no corner dark;
It is a lamp, a small and patient one,
That shows the next three steps, and not the park,
Nor all the city, nor the distant sea —
Just stone, and stair, and where the path will bend.

Not more, but less; the dark has no clear end.
So carry it, he said, and carry low,
And do not curse the shadows at your side;
The ones who walk most surely do not know
The whole road — only that the lamp is wide
Enough for one more step, and one, and one,
Until the walking is the journey done.

passage.title: Should Social Media Have a Minimum Age of 16?
paras: **Viewpoint 1 — Dr. Amal, child psychologist:** I see the effects every week: teenagers comparing themselves with filtered images, losing sleep to endless scrolling, and being bullied in ways that follow them home. Some countries have begun introducing minimum ages of 16 for social media. Younger teenagers are still developing the judgement needed to manage these pressures. A higher age limit would give them time to grow before facing them.

**Viewpoint 2 — Yazeed, 17, student:** Social media is where my generation talks, learns and creates. I learned graphic design from online tutorials and found friends who share my interests. A ban would not remove the risks; it would push younger users to lie about their age or use less safe platforms. Instead of banning teenagers, we should teach digital skills in school and require platforms to design safer features.

passage.title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
paras: When a map app shows your position as a small blue dot, it is relying on a network of satellites orbiting about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. The best-known system is GPS, operated by the United States, but several others exist.

Each satellite carries an extremely precise atomic clock and continuously broadcasts its position and the exact time. A receiver in your phone picks up these signals and calculates how long each one took to arrive. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, the delay reveals the distance to each satellite. With signals from at least four satellites, the receiver can work out its position in three dimensions and correct its own less precise clock — a process related to **trilateration**.

Precision matters enormously. An error of just one millionth of a second would place you about 300 metres from your real position. The system must even account for Einstein’s theories of relativity: because the satellites move fast and experience weaker gravity, their clocks run at a slightly different rate from clocks on the ground, by about 38 millionths of a second per day. Without correction, positions would drift by kilometres each day.

The same signals that guide drivers also help time financial transactions, coordinate power grids and track ships at sea, making satellite navigation one of the most important invisible technologies of modern life.
